content.text: Why do some components get hot when current flows through them? Why do different wires carry different amounts of current at the same voltage? The answer is resistance—the opposition to the flow of current. Understanding resistance is crucial for designing circuits that work safely and efficiently.
Resistance is the opposition to current flow, measured in ohms (Ω). It depends on the length, cross-sectional area, material, and temperature of a conductor.

When calculating resistance, always check your units. Length must be in metres (m) and cross-sectional area in square metres (m²). A common error is forgetting to convert mm² to m².

Superconductors are materials that have zero resistance when cooled below a critical temperature. They are used in MRI scanners and particle accelerators where large currents must flow without energy loss.
— Current (rate of flow) is the same throughout a series circuit. Resistance reduces the current for a given voltage.
— Parallel resistors combine to give less resistance, not more. Think of it as providing more paths.
— Thick wires have less resistance. More cross-sectional area means more paths for electrons.
— Resistors are essential for controlling current and voltage in circuits. Heating elements rely on resistance.
— Superconductors have exactly zero resistance below their critical temperature.

Adding a resistor in parallel provides an additional path for current. More paths means more total current can flow for the same voltage, which is equivalent to lower total resistance. Mathematically, 1/R_T = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... always gives R_T less than the smallest R.
